opus-5.5.text:
I think they're somewhat useful, but mostly as rough context rather than as tight benchmarks. Before we started doing these surveys, there were a handful of earlier efforts, things like informal polls at conferences, Michie's survey back in the seventies, and later Müller and Bostrom's survey. They give you a sense that people have been asking roughly this question for a long time and getting answers in roughly a similar range, which is interesting in itself.

The trouble is that they're hard to compare directly. The questions are worded differently, the definitions of human-level AI differ, the populations differ. Sometimes it's a small group at one event, sometimes it's people who self-selected into answering. And we've found in our own surveys that framing effects are huge. If you ask people for the year by which there's a fifty percent chance of something, versus asking what the probability is by a given year, you get quite different answers. Small changes in how you describe the milestone shift things a lot too. So if a framing effect within one survey is that large, comparing across surveys with different wording is pretty fraught.

That's actually a big part of why we try to keep our questions as consistent as possible from one round to the next. Our own earlier surveys end up being the most useful reference point, because then if the numbers move you can be more confident it reflects a real change in opinion rather than an artifact of question design. The older surveys are more like a historical backdrop, a reminder of how long people have been predicting this sort of thing and, honestly, a bit of humility about how much weight to put on any single set of expert forecasts.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier surveys are hard to compare directly because “the definitions of human-level AI differ.”

fable-5.1.text:
They're useful, but maybe not in the way people expect. The main thing earlier surveys gave us was a sense of what questions had already been asked and how researchers tended to interpret them, which is really valuable because a lot of the hard part of surveying is figuring out which framings produce coherent answers and which ones just produce noise. When we ran the first big one in 2016, we were partly building on things like the Müller and Bostrom survey and some of the older expert polls, and we deliberately kept some question wording stable so we could compare across time rather than just getting a snapshot.

That said, I'd be cautious about treating the older results as strong reference points for the actual numbers. The populations surveyed were different, often much smaller, and sometimes selected in ways that probably skewed toward people who already thought about these questions a lot. And we've seen in our own work that small changes in how you phrase a question, like asking about "high-level machine intelligence" versus "full automation of labor," can shift the median estimates by decades. So if the framing differs between surveys, the comparison gets pretty shaky.

Where I think they're genuinely useful is as evidence about trends in the field's mood. Even if any single survey is noisy, when you see timelines consistently shortening across several different efforts over a decade, that's harder to dismiss as an artifact. And they're a good reminder of how much expert opinion can move. People sometimes cite these numbers as if they were forecasts in a strong sense, and I think it's more honest to treat them as a measurement of what researchers believe at a given moment, which is interesting partly because it changes.

r001.rationale: The response says that differing question framings, such as “high-level machine intelligence” versus “full automation of labor,” can shift estimates and make comparisons between surveys shaky.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful, especially if you want to understand how people’s views are changing over time. You want to ask the same question, if you can, because otherwise it’s hard to tell whether people have changed their minds or whether they’re just responding differently to different wording.

But that creates a bit of a tension. You might look at an earlier question and think, well, I would have asked this differently. And then you have to choose between improving the question and keeping that comparison. One thing you can do is ask different versions to different groups of respondents, so you can get some sense of how much the wording matters.

So I’d treat earlier surveys as useful reference points, but I’d be cautious about putting all the results on one timeline and assuming they’re measuring exactly the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response says differing question wording can make survey results hard to compare, but it does not mention differing definitions of human-level AI across surveys.

sol-6.1.text: I find them useful, though there’s a tradeoff between keeping questions comparable and asking them in the way you think is best. If you change the wording, it becomes hard to tell whether a difference in answers reflects a change in people’s views or just a change in what you asked. So earlier surveys give us a starting point and a reason to repeat particular questions. But I wouldn’t treat their results as a precise baseline without looking carefully at who was surveyed and how the questions were framed.

r001.rationale: The response says changes in question wording make results hard to compare, but does not state that differing definitions of human-level AI across surveys cause the difficulty.
